title: Endometriosis: getting pain assessed and choosing care that fits your goals
intro: Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the womb lining growing outside the womb. It can cause inflammation, scarring, pelvic pain and fertility difficulties, although symptoms vary widely. Severe period pain that disrupts ordinary life deserves assessment, including in teenagers. It should not be dismissed as something you must tolerate or treated as a personal failure.

sections.heading: Recognise patterns without assuming every pain has one cause
paragraphs: Pain may occur around periods or at other times, during or after sex, bowel movements or urination. Fatigue, bloating and difficulty becoming pregnant may also occur. The amount of visible disease does not always match pain severity, and some people have few symptoms. Keep a manageable record of timing, bleeding, bowel or urinary symptoms, missed school or work and the effect of medicines. Mention family history and whether pregnancy is a current goal. Other conditions, including adenomyosis, infection, bowel disorders and ovarian problems, can overlap or need different treatment. Endometriosis is not contagious, and its cause is not fully understood.

sections.heading: A normal scan does not exclude endometriosis
paragraphs: A clinician takes a history and may offer an examination with your consent and an ultrasound, using an approach appropriate to your circumstances. You can ask for explanation, a chaperone, an alternative or to stop an examination. Specialist ultrasound or MRI may assess deep disease, ovarian cysts called endometriomas and involvement of bowel, bladder or ureters. Superficial disease can be missed on scans. Persistent symptoms or a major impact on daily life can justify referral despite normal imaging. Laparoscopy may be considered to investigate or treat disease, but surgery is not always required before starting symptom treatment. Ask what each proposed test can change and agree follow-up if the first approach does not help.

sections.heading: Pain treatment and hormones need an individual plan
paragraphs: Suitable painkillers may help, with advice about dose, duration, interactions and when to review rather than indefinite escalation. Hormonal options can reduce pain by suppressing disease activity or periods, including certain contraceptive or progestogen treatments. The choice depends on medical history, side effects, preferences and whether you are trying to conceive. Some specialist hormone treatments can cause low-oestrogen symptoms and affect bone health, requiring a clear monitoring and protective-treatment plan. Hormonal suppression is not a treatment to improve spontaneous pregnancy rates while trying for a baby. Do not assume every hormone preparation provides reliable contraception. Symptoms can recur after stopping treatment; ask how the plan will be reviewed.

sections.heading: Surgery and fertility decisions should be discussed together
paragraphs: Surgery may remove or destroy lesions, release adhesions or address an endometrioma, but benefits, recurrence and operative risks vary. Deep disease may need a specialist team with bowel or urinary expertise. Ovarian surgery can affect ovarian reserve, especially with repeat procedures, so discuss fertility before deciding. Some people benefit from fertility treatment rather than repeated surgery; age, other fertility factors and personal goals matter. Hysterectomy is not a guaranteed cure because disease may remain outside the womb, and removal of ovaries has additional consequences. Pregnancy is not a cure to recommend as treatment. Ask what is being removed, alternatives, the likely effect on pain and fertility, and support during recovery.

sections.heading: Support daily life and recognise symptoms that cannot wait
paragraphs: A pain service, appropriately trained pelvic physiotherapist, psychological support and practical school or work adjustments may help alongside medical treatment. This does not mean the pain is imaginary. Heat can be comforting when used safely without burns; no special diet or supplement is a proven universal cure. Sudden severe or worsening pelvic pain, fainting, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding or breathing difficulty needs emergency assessment, especially if pregnancy is possible. Pain with possible pregnancy also needs prompt advice because ectopic pregnancy must be considered. Fever, repeated vomiting or difficulty passing urine needs urgent assessment. Do not automatically attribute a new severe pattern to established endometriosis. Agree a plan for flares, ongoing review and referral when treatment is ineffective.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a normal scan is not the end of assessment
examples.text: Lina misses school each month because of pain. Her ultrasound is normal, but she returns with a symptom record and asks about referral and treatment. The team considers endometriosis and other causes rather than concluding that the pain cannot be real.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: fertility changes the discussion
examples.text: Mira has an ovarian endometrioma and wants to become pregnant. Before surgery she asks about ovarian reserve, alternatives and whether fertility assessment should happen first. She and the specialist choose a plan around her priorities rather than treating every cyst in the same way.
